channel.title: Acting UK London Fringe Theatre
channel.description: Acting UK London Fringe Theatre — original editorial coverage for UK actors.

item.title: On a small stage, there is nowhere for an actor to hide
item.description: An editorial reflection on proximity, scale and why fringe performance can make the smallest choice feel enormous.

item.title: The quiet virtuosity of stepping into someone else's part
item.description: An appreciation of covers, understudies and the craft of keeping a small production alive when its cast changes.

item.title: New writing needs an audience, not a verdict
item.description: Why the first public life of a new play is a conversation between writer, actors and a room full of strangers.

item.title: The Master Builder: ambition begins to look like fear
item.description: Greg Hicks stars in David Edgar’s version of Ibsen at the Arcola, where the older artist’s dread of being replaced remains painfully current.

item.title: Sirocco: the Noël Coward play that refused to behave
item.description: The Finborough revisits Coward’s notorious early failure, restoring censored material and asking whether a scandal can outlive its original audience.

item.title: Cranford: the quiet art of making a room laugh
item.description: Tamsin Greig leads an ensemble in Richmond, where Elizabeth Gaskell’s village becomes a study in comic timing and private grief.

item.title: Roleplay: when the personal brand becomes the part
item.description: Hannah Reilly’s solo show reaches its final week at Soho Theatre, with critics admiring the performer more consistently than the play.

item.title: Wits End: a funeral with rather too much unfinished business
item.description: Estée Stimler’s family comedy puts grief and obligation in a room of fifty-five seats.

item.title: Attention: the art of listening when the script can change
item.description: Jules Head and Georgia Bruce bring their formally adventurous two-hander to the Bush Studio, with its original Dublin cast.

item.title: Doublespeak: the classics have a few things to say about spin
item.description: A new early modern theatre festival in Camberwell gives emerging performers a chance to examine the politics of language.

item.title: The Café: a little shelter in a city that rarely sits still
item.description: Roccia Zhang’s multilingual play brings four London lives together at the Etcetera Theatre during Voila! Theatre Festival.

item.title: Horrible Things: Frankie Thompson makes discomfort a comic instrument
item.description: Two critics consider the clown’s unsettling, inventive solo show, now at Soho Theatre until 21 November.

item.title: Lear: Ian McKellen returns to a role that refuses to let him go
item.description: A new play at the Yard Theatre brings Shakespeare into conversation with the actor’s own working life, opening on 17 November.

item.title: Lover Girl: Temi Wilkey takes the solo show into stranger territory
item.description: Critical responses differ over the structure of Wilkey’s solo performance, blending stand-up, R&B and theatrical surrealism at Soho Upstairs.

item.title: Relative Motion: when a romance starts obeying different laws
item.description: Stephanie Greenwood’s new play uses physics to examine a relationship that moves from attraction towards coercion.

item.title: Dogstar: a stranded crew, a restless new playwright and divided critics
item.description: Daisy Hall’s Arctic-set dark comedy at Hampstead Downstairs has drawn contrasting responses, with praise for its three performers.

item.title: A wrong turn on the way home from IKEA leads to Dante’s dark wood
item.description: Tania Khan’s I Can See the Sun brings surreal new writing to the Hope Theatre in Islington, with remaining performances through 21 November.

item.title: The Moth: can two men ever escape the history that binds them?
item.description: Paul Herzberg’s London premiere at the Finborough has inspired contrasting critical reactions to its exploration of apartheid and forgiveness.
